claim: Asynchronous transmission plays a prominent role at certain synapses.
source: Asynchronous transmission plays a prominent role at certain synapses but lacks the mechanistic insights of its synchronous counterpart.
evidence: This is a general statement about asynchronous transmission supported by established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Asynchronous transmission lacks the mechanistic insights of its synchronous counterpart.
source: Asynchronous transmission plays a prominent role at certain synapses but lacks the mechanistic insights of its synchronous counterpart.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The current view posits that triggering of asynchronous release during repetitive stimulation involves expansion of the same calcium domains underlying synchronous transmission.
source: The current view posits that triggering of asynchronous release during repetitive stimulation involves expansion of the same calcium domains underlying synchronous transmission.
evidence: This describes the prevailing hypothesis in the field, which is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Synchronous release is tied to calcium entry into synaptic boutons via P/Q type calcium channels at the zebrafish neuromuscular synapse.
source: Synchronous release is tied to calcium entry into synaptic boutons via P/Q type calcium channels, whereas asynchronous release is boosted by a propagating intracellular calcium source initiated at off-synaptic locations in the axon and axonal branch points.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including pharmacological blockade experiments and calcium imaging.

claim: Asynchronous release is boosted by a propagating intracellular calcium source initiated at off-synaptic locations in the axon and axonal branch points at the zebrafish neuromuscular synapse.
source: Synchronous release is tied to calcium entry into synaptic boutons via P/Q type calcium channels, whereas asynchronous release is boosted by a propagating intracellular calcium source initiated at off-synaptic locations in the axon and axonal branch points.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by live calcium imaging and paired patch clamp recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The secondary calcium source fully accounts for the persistence of asynchronous release following termination of the stimulus.
source: This secondary calcium source fully accounts for the persistence following termination of the stimulus and sensitivity to slow calcium buffers reported for asynchronous release.
evidence: This is supported by killswitch experiments shown in Figure 8 where release persists after stimulus termination.

claim: The secondary calcium source fully accounts for the sensitivity to slow calcium buffers reported for asynchronous release.
source: This secondary calcium source fully accounts for the persistence following termination of the stimulus and sensitivity to slow calcium buffers reported for asynchronous release.
evidence: This is supported by EGTA experiments shown in Figures 9 and 10 demonstrating EGTA sensitivity of asynchronous release.

claim: The neuromuscular junction and CNS neurons share features related to asynchronous release.
source: The neuromuscular junction and CNS neurons share these features, raising the possibility that secondary calcium sources are common among synapses with prominent asynchronous release.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published literature on CNS neurons and the authors' findings.

claim: Secondary calcium sources may be common among synapses with prominent asynchronous release.
source: The neuromuscular junction and CNS neurons share these features, raising the possibility that secondary calcium sources are common among synapses with prominent asynchronous release.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings and comparison with other systems.

claim: At most synapses, the asynchronous contribution to release is smaller than the synchronous component.
source: At most synapses, the asynchronous contribution to release is smaller than the synchronous component, but becomes more prominent with repetitive stimulation (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Lu and Trussell, 2000; Hefft and Jonas, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Asynchronous release becomes more prominent with repetitive stimulation.
source: At most synapses, the asynchronous contribution to release is smaller than the synchronous component, but becomes more prominent with repetitive stimulation (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Lu and Trussell, 2000; Hefft and Jonas, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by the authors' own data in Figure 1.

claim: Asynchronous release may provide persistent transmitter release under conditions where phase locking to the action potential is not required.
source: Little is known about the functional significance, but the most widely held idea is that it provides persistent transmitter release under conditions where phase locking to the action potential is not required (Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Hefft and Jonas, 2005; Best and Regehr, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: At the zebrafish neuromuscular junction, asynchronous release may augment release during bouts of prolonged swimming, where release probability may be severely compromised.
source: At the zebrafish neuromuscular junction (NMJ), asynchronous release may augment release during bouts of prolonged swimming, where release probability may be severely compromised.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Synchronous release is triggered by highly localized calcium transients resulting from the opening of calcium channels near the active zones.
source: According to this idea, synchronous release is triggered by highly localized calcium transients resulting from the opening of calcium channels near the active zones (Adler et al., 1991; Stanley, 1993; Neher, 1998; Meinrenken et al., 2002; Augustine et al., 2003; Eggermann et al., 2012), whereas a more slowly decaying component of intracellular calcium is proposed to account for the asynchronous release (Rahamimoff and Yaari, 1973; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Cummings et al., 1996; Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Chen and Regehr, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: A more slowly decaying component of intracellular calcium is proposed to account for asynchronous release.
source: According to this idea, synchronous release is triggered by highly localized calcium transients resulting from the opening of calcium channels near the active zones (Adler et al., 1991; Stanley, 1993; Neher, 1998; Meinrenken et al., 2002; Augustine et al., 2003; Eggermann et al., 2012), whereas a more slowly decaying component of intracellular calcium is proposed to account for the asynchronous release (Rahamimoff and Yaari, 1973; Goda and Stevens, 1994; Cummings et al., 1996; Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Chen and Regehr, 1999).
evidence: This is the prevailing hypothesis in the field supported by multiple citations.

claim: The slow accumulation of calcium during repeated stimulation can potentially account for both the delayed onset and persistence of asynchronous release.
source: The slow accumulation of calcium during repeated stimulation can potentially account for both the delayed onset and persistence (Lu and Trussell, 2000; Hefft and Jonas, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The slow calcium buffer EGTA can block asynchronous release while leaving synchronous release intact.
source: Much of the evidence for this idea rests on the observation that the slow calcium buffer EGTA can block asynchronous release while leaving synchronous release intact (Adler et al., 1991; Cummings et al., 1996; Atluri and Regehr, 1998; Lu and Trussell, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: The faster calcium buffer BAPTA is required to inhibit synchronous release.
source: The fact that the faster calcium buffer BAPTA is required to inhibit synchronous release has been interpreted to represent a more restricted calcium domain that is in close vicinity to the calcium sensors underlying exocytosis (Neher, 1998; Eggermann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: BAPTA requirement for blocking synchronous release represents a more restricted calcium domain that is in close vicinity to the calcium sensors underlying exocytosis.
source: The fact that the faster calcium buffer BAPTA is required to inhibit synchronous release has been interpreted to represent a more restricted calcium domain that is in close vicinity to the calcium sensors underlying exocytosis (Neher, 1998; Eggermann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation from the literature supported by citations.

claim: There has been little consideration of alternative secondary sources of calcium for asynchronous release, despite evidence for their involvement in synaptic transmission.
source: There has been little consideration of alternative secondary sources of calcium, despite evidence for their involvement in synaptic transmission (Collin et al., 2005; Berridge, 2006).
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: An unusual voltage dependent calcium channel type provides persistent calcium entry for asynchronous release in one recent case.
source: In one recent case however, an unexpected source of calcium for asynchronous release was reported in the form of an unusual voltage dependent calcium channel type that provides persistent calcium entry (Few et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: A block of calcium entry through the presynaptic P/Q calcium channels fully inhibited synchronous release, leaving asynchronous release intact at the zebrafish NMJ.
source: Our investigation into possible separate sources of calcium in zebrafish motor neurons was prompted by our observation that a block of calcium entry through the presynaptic P/Q calcium channels fully inhibited synchronous release, leaving asynchronous release intact.
evidence: This is a key observation from the authors' experiments, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Paired patch clamp recordings from the caudal primary motor neuron (CaP) and target fast skeletal muscle showed a stereotypic transition from exclusively synchronous to principally asynchronous transmission when stimulated at frequencies greater than 20 Hz.
source: Paired patch clamp recordings from the caudal primary motor neuron (CaP) and target fast skeletal muscle showed a stereotypic transition from exclusively synchronous to principally asynchronous transmission when stimulated at frequencies greater than 20 Hz (Figure 1A,B; Wen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and a previous publication.

claim: Behaviorally evoked contractures of zebrafish axial muscle correspond to frequencies between 20 Hz and 100 Hz.
source: Behaviorally evoked contractures of zebrafish axial muscle correspond to frequencies between 20 Hz and 100 Hz, so we continue to use the latter stimulus frequency as the benchmark for our studies.
evidence: This is a physiological observation that provides context for the experimental design.

claim: At 100 Hz, greater than 95% of the synaptic responses were phase locked to the presynaptic action potential during the first second of stimulation.
source: At 100 Hz, greater than 95% of the synaptic responses were phase locked to the presynaptic action potential during the first second of stimulation (Figure 1A1,B; Wen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and a previous publication.

claim: The onset of asynchronous release occurred after the first second of stimulation, displaying a time-dependent increase in overall contribution during the ensuing stimulation.
source: The onset of asynchronous release occurred after the first second of stimulation, displaying a time-dependent increase in overall contribution during the ensuing stimulation (Figure 1A2,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Each of the two modes (synchronous and asynchronous) accounted for approximately half of the total synaptic transmission.
source: The release associated with synchronous vs asynchronous events showed a time-dependent transition, and overall each of the two modes accounted for approximately half of the total synaptic transmission (Figure 1B; Wen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1B and a previous publication.

claim: The amplitudes of the asynchronous events were indistinguishable from the spontaneous synaptic events measured in the absence of stimulation.
source: The amplitudes of the asynchronous events were indistinguishable from the spontaneous synaptic events measured in the absence of stimulation (Figure 1C), consistent with each representing individual quanta.
evidence: This is supported by amplitude distribution analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Each asynchronous event represents individual quanta.
source: The amplitudes of the asynchronous events were indistinguishable from the spontaneous synaptic events measured in the absence of stimulation (Figure 1C), consistent with each representing individual quanta.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in amplitude distributions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Synchronous release is strictly dependent on P/Q-type calcium channel function.
source: The synchronous release is strictly dependent on P/Q-type calcium channel function (Figure 1D; Wen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and a previous publication.

claim: Inhibiting P/Q calcium channels with 1 µM ω-conotoxin GVIA nearly abolished synchronous release.
source: Inhibiting P/Q calcium channels with 1 µM ω-conotoxin GVIA nearly abolished synchronous release (Figure 1D1,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D1 and 1E.

claim: Asynchronous release remained intact in the ω-conotoxin GVIA treated fish, but with a greatly delayed onset compared to the control fish.
source: Unexpectedly, asynchronous release remained intact in the ω-conotoxin GVIA treated fish, but with a greatly delayed onset compared to the control fish (Figure 1D2,E).
evidence: This is a key finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D2 and 1E.

claim: Over 85% of release seen in ω-conotoxin GVIA fish was associated with the asynchronous mode.
source: Quantitatively, over 85% of release seen in ω-conotoxin GVIA fish was associated with the asynchronous mode, and this likely represents an underestimate because of the resolution of our analysis (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The motility mutant line tb204a has greatly compromised P/Q calcium channel function but is not a complete null.
source: The motility mutant line tb204a has greatly compromised P/Q calcium channel function but is not a complete null (Wen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a previous publication characterizing the mutant.

claim: In tb204a mutant, the synchronous release was reduced but not eliminated completely.
source: Accordingly, the synchronous release was reduced but not eliminated completely (Figure 1G1), leaving asynchronous release intact (Figure 1G2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G1.

claim: In tb204a mutant, asynchronous release was left intact.
source: Accordingly, the synchronous release was reduced but not eliminated completely (Figure 1G1), leaving asynchronous release intact (Figure 1G2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G2.

claim: The tb204a mutant showed both reduced synchronous release and delayed onset of asynchronous release compared to control.
source: Quantitation of the time-dependent contributions showed both reduced synchronous release and delayed onset of asynchronous release for tb204a compared to control (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The time to peak release was largest for ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated, smallest for control, and intermediate for tb204a mutant fish.
source: When expressed as the time required to reach peak response during the stimulus train, the values were largest for ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated, smallest for control, and intermediate for tb204a mutant fish (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The time to peak release for ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish and tb204a mutant were significantly prolonged when compared to control (p<0.001).
source: The time to peak release for ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish and tb204a mutant were much more variable than seen in control fish, but despite the variability both were significantly prolonged when compared to control (p<0.001; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stimulation of CaP motor neurons for 10 s at 100 Hz resulted in a robust fluorescence increase that was largely restricted to the boutons associated with synapses.
source: Stimulation of CaP motor neurons for 10 s at 100 Hz resulted in a robust fluorescence increase that was largely restricted to the boutons associated with synapses (Figure 3A, spH).
evidence: This is supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fluorescence for control ROIs rose immediately at the start of 100 Hz stimulation and reached a plateau during the subsequent few seconds of stimulation.
source: The fluorescence for control ROIs rose immediately at the start of 100 Hz stimulation and reached a plateau during the subsequent few seconds of stimulation (gray traces, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fluorescence signal in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neurons showed greatly delayed onset of fluorescence for comparable ROIs.
source: However, the fluorescence signal in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neurons showed greatly delayed onset of fluorescence for comparable ROIs (color traces, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The synaptopHluorin signal was reduced in the ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish.
source: Additionally, the synaptopHluorin signal was reduced in the ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by synaptopHluorin imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The distribution of time to 50% maximal intensity showed non-overlapping values for control and ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish.
source: The distribution showed non-overlapping values for control and ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In control neurons, ΔG/R within the axon initial segment and distal boutons showed no significant difference in the timing of signal onset.
source: In control neurons, ΔG/R within the axon initial segment and distal boutons showed no significant difference in the timing of signal onset (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: In fish treated with ω-conotoxin GVIA, the fluorescent signal onset was delayed for all regions except the axon initial segment.
source: By contrast, in fish treated with ω-conotoxin GVIA, the fluorescent signal onset was delayed for all regions except the axon initial segment (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: In ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish, the delay in calcium signal onset was longer with greater distance from the soma.
source: Moreover, the delay was longer with greater distance from the soma (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: With both Fluo-4 and Fluo-5F the time to 20% rise was significantly longer in ω-conotoxin GVIA treated fish compared to control fish.
source: With both Fluo-4 and Fluo-5F the time to 20% rise was significantly longer in ω-conotoxin GVIA treated fish compared to control fish (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: There was no significant difference between Fluo-4 and Fluo-5F dyes in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish.
source: Importantly, there was no significant difference between the dyes in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: The time to 20% rise was marginally different (p=0.01) between Fluo-4 and Fluo-5F dyes in control experiments.
source: The time to 20% rise was marginally different (p=0.01) between the dyes in control experiments, potentially reflecting the increased time required for the lower affinity calcium indicators to measure the calcium rise.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: A striking quasi-linear relationship was observed between time to 20% rise and distance from the reference point for boutons in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neurons.
source: When expressed as time to 20% rise vs distance from the reference point, a striking quasi-linear relationship was observed for the boutons (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The mean velocity of calcium signal travel obtained in boutons determined for the cumulative data was 74 μm/s in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish.
source: The mean velocity of travel obtained in boutons determined for the cumulative data was 74 μm/s in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish.
evidence: This is calculated from the slope of the distance vs time relationship shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In control neurons, the relationships obtained showed no dependence on distance in keeping with velocity of the propagating action potential.
source: By contrast, the relationships obtained for control neurons showed no dependence on distance in keeping with velocity of the propagating action potential (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neurons the distance dependence was not observed for the proximal axon.
source: In ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neurons the distance dependence was not observed for the proximal axon, suggesting that the signaling underlying calcium propagation in these regions may be different from that of the distal terminals (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: The signaling underlying calcium propagation in proximal axon regions may be different from that of the distal terminals.
source: In ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neurons the distance dependence was not observed for the proximal axon, suggesting that the signaling underlying calcium propagation in these regions may be different from that of the distal terminals (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is inferred from the different distance-dependence patterns observed in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: In seven paired recordings with 5 mM intracellular EGTA using a killswitch protocol, the asynchronous release persisted well beyond termination of the stimulus.
source: In seven such recordings with 5 mM intracellular EGTA, the asynchronous release persisted well beyond termination of the stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by killswitch experiments shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: The calcium signal measured using Fluo-4 in the presence of 0.5 mM EGTA exhibited distance-dependent onset with the signal in the distal boutons peaking following termination of the stimulus.
source: The calcium signal, measured using Fluo-4 in the presence of 0.5 mM EGTA, also exhibited distance-dependent onset with the signal in the distal boutons peaking following termination of the stimulus (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The findings strongly support the involvement of a propagating calcium signal that was triggered by stimulation at the soma.
source: Because the stimulus was terminated prematurely in both paired recordings and calcium measurements, continued accumulation would not occur and could not account for the delayed onset of asynchronous release and the calcium signal. Instead, the findings strongly support the involvement of a propagating calcium signal that was triggered by stimulation at the soma.
evidence: This is inferred from the killswitch experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: In three separate simultaneous recordings, the onset time for the calcium signal and asynchronous release, both measured at 50% rise, was within 0.4 ± 0.3 s of each other.
source: In three separate simultaneous recordings, the onset time for the calcium signal and asynchronous release, both measured at 50% rise, was within 0.4 ± 0.3 s of each other.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous paired recording and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9.

claim: A large difference in delay of onset was seen between experiments performed with 0.5 mM EGTA and 5 mM EGTA in the internal solution.
source: Additionally, a large difference in delay of onset was seen between experiments performed with 0.5 mM EGTA (Figure 9A–D) and 5 mM EGTA (Figure 9E–H) in the internal solution, prompting further investigation into the dependence of the calcium propagation on calcium buffering.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 9A-D vs 9E-H.

claim: For ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish, calcium measurement from ROIs corresponding to boutons showed two to threefold greater delay in signal onset with 5 mM EGTA compared to 0.5 mM EGTA.
source: For ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish, calcium measurement from ROIs corresponding to boutons showed two to threefold greater delay in signal onset with 5 mM EGTA (red) compared to 0.5 mM EGTA (blue, Figure 10A; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10A and Table 1.

claim: The mean values obtained using 5 mM EGTA were significantly larger at all distances than those obtained using 0.5 mM EGTA for toxin treated fish (p<0.001).
source: Overall, the mean values obtained using 5 mM EGTA were significantly larger at all distances than those obtained using 0.5 mM EGTA for toxin treated fish (Figure 10B, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Fitting distance vs rise in the regions corresponding to boutons to a linear relationship yielded mean slope values corresponding to 74 μm/s and 35 μm/s for 0.5 mM and 5 mM EGTA respectively.
source: Fitting distance vs rise in the regions corresponding to boutons to a linear relationship yielded mean slope values corresponding to 74 μm/s and 35 μm/s for 0.5 mM and 5 mM EGTA respectively, consistent with a slower propagating rate in the presence of greater Ca2+ buffer (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is calculated from the slope analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The slower propagating rate is consistent with the presence of greater Ca2+ buffer.
source: Fitting distance vs rise in the regions corresponding to boutons to a linear relationship yielded mean slope values corresponding to 74 μm/s and 35 μm/s for 0.5 mM and 5 mM EGTA respectively, consistent with a slower propagating rate in the presence of greater Ca2+ buffer (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of propagation velocities at different EGTA concentrations.

claim: At both EGTA concentrations, the arrival of the calcium signal in the axonal regions appeared to be independent of distance from the stimulation.
source: At both the EGTA concentrations, the arrival of the calcium signal in the axonal regions appeared to be independent of distance from the stimulation, despite the large differences in onset time.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The distance-independence of calcium signal arrival in axonal regions is indicative of a faster velocity of travel along these regions of the neuron.
source: These data are indicative of a faster velocity of travel along these regions of the neuron.
evidence: This is inferred from the distance-independence observed in the axonal regions.

claim: In control fish, the distance-dependence of calcium signal onset was not seen.
source: In control fish, the distance-dependence of calcium signal onset was not seen (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: In control fish, 5 mM EGTA slowed the time to 20% rise in calcium signal compared to 0.5 mM EGTA (p<0.001).
source: However, 5 mM EGTA slowed the time to 20% rise in calcium signal compared to 0.5 mM EGTA, reflecting the competition between the indicator and the calcium buffer (Table 1, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: In the presence of ω-conotoxin GVIA, the time to peak release was greater than twofold larger in the presence of 5 mM EGTA compared to 0.5 mM EGTA.
source: In the presence of ω-conotoxin GVIA, where release is exclusively asynchronous, the time to peak release was greater than twofold larger in the presence of 5 mM EGTA compared to 0.5 mM EGTA (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Inclusion of 25 mM EGTA in the electrode eliminated the majority of synaptic transmission in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish in all but one recording.
source: Inclusion of 25 mM EGTA in the electrode eliminated the majority of synaptic transmission in ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated fish in all but the single recording shown, where the onset of asynchronous release is further delayed compared with those recorded in 5 mM EGTA (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The overall data for all recordings at 0.5 mM and 5 mM EGTA shows a highly significant difference in the time to peak release.
source: The overall data for all of the recordings at 0.5 mM and 5 mM EGTA shows a highly significant difference in the time to peak release (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 10E.

claim: In control recordings the time to peak release was slightly higher for 5 mM EGTA (p=0.01).
source: In control recordings the time to peak release was slightly higher for 5 mM EGTA (Table 1, p=0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Treatment with high concentrations of Cd2+ (500 μM) required to inhibit the propagating calcium signals also inhibited the sodium channels responsible for action potential propagation.
source: The high concentrations (500 μM) required to inhibit the propagating calcium signals also inhibited the sodium channels responsible for action potential propagation, so firm conclusions could not be drawn.
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The T-type calcium channel inhibitors Mibefradil (5 µM) together with Ni2+ (100 µM) effectively reduced the calcium signal in the axon and boutons.
source: The rather non-specific T-type calcium channel inhibitors Mibefradil (5 µM) together with Ni2+ (100 µM) effectively reduced the calcium signal in the axon and boutons as did the L-type blocker Nimodipine (50 µM).
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The L-type blocker Nimodipine (50 µM) effectively reduced the calcium signal in the axon and boutons.
source: The rather non-specific T-type calcium channel inhibitors Mibefradil (5 µM) together with Ni2+ (100 µM) effectively reduced the calcium signal in the axon and boutons as did the L-type blocker Nimodipine (50 µM).
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Other L-type blockers Nitrendipine (25 µM), Nifedipine (50 µM) and Isradipine (50 µM) were without effect on calcium signal.
source: However, other L-type blockers Nitrendipine (25 µM), Nifedipine (50 µM) and Isradipine (50 µM) were without effect.
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The R-type Ca2+ channel blocker SNX 482 (200 nM) was completely ineffective on calcium signal.
source: Similarly, the R-type Ca2+ channel blocker SNX 482 (200 nM) was completely ineffective.
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The calcium stores inhibitor thapsigargin (1 µM) was without effect on calcium signal.
source: The calcium stores inhibitor thapsigargin (1 µM) and the IP3 receptor antagonists 2-APB (50 µM) and Xestospongin-C (5 µM) were also without effect.
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The IP3 receptor antagonists 2-APB (50 µM) and Xestospongin-C (5 µM) were without effect on calcium signal.
source: The calcium stores inhibitor thapsigargin (1 µM) and the IP3 receptor antagonists 2-APB (50 µM) and Xestospongin-C (5 µM) were also without effect.
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Ruthenium red (400 µM) and ryanodine (100 µM), inhibitors of the ryanodine receptors, gave variable results, only in some cases appearing to increase the arrival time for calcium in the boutons.
source: Both ruthenium red (400 µM) and ryanodine (100 µM), inhibitors of the ryanodine receptors, gave variable results, only in some cases appearing to increase the arrival time for calcium in the boutons.
evidence: This is an observation from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Prolonged depolarization of the CaP motor neuron in the presence of 1 μM TTX resulted in a calcium propagation that was clearly followed from soma to boutons without failure.
source: Prolonged depolarization of the CaP motor neuron in the presence of 1 μM TTX resulted in a calcium propagation that was clearly followed from soma to boutons without failure (Video 3; Figure 11A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 3 and Figure 11A.

claim: In most TTX recordings, multiple propagating signals were observed in the boutons.
source: In most recordings, multiple propagating signals were observed in the boutons (Video 3; Figure 11B) and occasionally the signal back-propagated to the soma (Video 4) rendering difficult the measurements of velocity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Videos 3 and 4 and Figure 11B.

claim: In the TTX experiment shown in Figure 11, the forward propagating velocity for the first propagating signal corresponded to 3 μm/s.
source: However, in the case shown in Figure 11 (Video 3), the forward propagating velocity for the first propagating signal corresponded to 3 μm/s.
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Overall estimates of calcium propagation velocity in TTX fall between 3–10 μm/s.
source: Overall estimates fall between 3–10 μm/s that is considerably slower than those obtained with ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neuron (Figures 7 and 10).
evidence: This is based on analysis of multiple TTX experiments.

claim: The calcium propagation velocity in TTX (3-10 μm/s) is considerably slower than those obtained with ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neuron (74 μm/s).
source: Overall estimates fall between 3–10 μm/s that is considerably slower than those obtained with ω-conotoxin GVIA-treated neuron (Figures 7 and 10).
evidence: This is a comparison of velocities calculated from different experimental conditions.

claim: The difference in propagation velocity between TTX and ω-conotoxin GVIA conditions points to a dominant role of the axonal action potential in coordinating the calcium signaling in the axon initiation zone and the axon proper.
source: This difference points to a dominant role of the axonal action potential in coordinating the calcium signaling in the axon initiation zone and the axon proper.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of propagation velocities under different conditions.

claim: The prevailing view that asynchronous release results exclusively from an expansion of the highly restricted calcium domains surrounding the same calcium channels that govern synchronous release is challenged by a model with separate, but interactive calcium sources.
source: A model with separate, but interactive calcium sources, challenges the prevailing view that asynchronous release results exclusively from an expansion of the highly restricted calcium domains surrounding the same calcium channels that govern synchronous release (Borst and Sakmann, 1996; Meinrenken et al., 2002).
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their findings in the context of existing literature.

claim: The expanding domain model would predict that blocking the source of calcium for synchronous release would also inhibit the asynchronous release.
source: This model would predict that blocking the source of calcium for synchronous release would also inhibit the asynchronous release.
evidence: This is a logical prediction from the prevailing model.

claim: The differential sensitivity of synchronous vs asynchronous release to slow calcium buffers provides support for an expanding domain model.
source: Support for an expanding domain comes principally from the differential sensitivity of synchronous vs asynchronous release to slow calcium buffers (Neher, 1998; Eggermann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The BAPTA/EGTA efficacy criteria has been used successfully to probe local calcium signaling with the conclusion that high BAPTA/EGTA efficacy points toward nanodomain and equal efficacy implicates diffuse calcium signals or microdomains.
source: Augustine notes that 'this criteria has been used successfully to probe local calcium signaling with the conclusion that high BAPTA/EGTA efficacy points toward nanodomain and equal efficacy implicates diffuse calcium signals or microdomains' (Augustine et al., 2003), an approach widely used as a determinant of calcium channel-calcium sensor coupling (Eggermann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established methodology from the literature supported by citations.

claim: At zebrafish NMJ, asynchronous release is highly sensitive to the slow buffer EGTA.
source: It is the case with zebrafish NMJ that asynchronous release, as well as the calcium propagation, is highly sensitive to the slow buffer EGTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: At zebrafish NMJ, calcium propagation is highly sensitive to the slow buffer EGTA.
source: It is the case with zebrafish NMJ that asynchronous release, as well as the calcium propagation, is highly sensitive to the slow buffer EGTA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: The differential EGTA sensitivity at zebrafish NMJ reflects, to a large extent, the involvement of bulk cytoplasmic changes stemming from distal calcium as opposed solely to highly restricted calcium domains entering through the P/Q type calcium channels.
source: We interpret these findings to mean that in zebrafish the differential sensitivity reflects, to a large extent, the involvement of bulk cytoplasmic changes stemming from distal calcium as opposed solely to highly restricted calcium domains entering through the P/Q type calcium channels.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental findings.

claim: The interpretation of EGTA sensitivity provides an alternative to the BAPTA/EGTA sensitivity metric but does not exclude additional contribution by the expanding zone of calcium formed by local P/Q channel openings.
source: This provides an alternative interpretation to the BAPTA/EGTA sensitivity metric but does not exclude additional contribution by the expanding zone of calcium formed by local P/Q channel openings.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation acknowledging both their findings and existing models.

claim: The pharmacological results point to no clear source of either intracellular or extracellular calcium as required for the initiation or propagation.
source: The pharmacological results point to no clear source of either intracellular or extracellular calcium as required for the initiation or propagation.
evidence: This is a summary of the pharmacological experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The calcium propagation is so potent in the branch points and locations near boutons that there may be a large safety factor that requires near extinction of calcium before propagation is terminated.
source: One impression resulting from these experiments is that the propagation is so potent in the branch points and locations near boutons, that there may be a large safety factor that requires near extinction of calcium before propagation is terminated.
evidence: This is speculated based on the difficulty in blocking calcium propagation pharmacologically.

claim: TTX experiments provide insights that Ca2+ propagation can be elicited with prolonged depolarization in the absence of action potentials, but the apparent velocity is slow.
source: Our results from TTX experiments provide some insights into the process of calcium propagation. In the absence of action potentials, Ca2+ propagation can be elicited with prolonged depolarization, but the apparent velocity is slow.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 11 and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Ca2+ propagation is less dependent on coordination by the action potential in the boutons than in the axons.
source: These data are compatible with a model in which Ca2+ propagation is less dependent on coordination by the action potential in the boutons than in the axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the TTX experiments showing different propagation characteristics.

claim: An action potential traveling down the axon would instantaneously initiate Ca2+ propagation at the branching point, whereas the spread of depolarization would take much longer in the presence of TTX.
source: Accordingly, an action potential traveling down the axon would instantaneously initiate Ca2+ propagation at the branching point, whereas the spread of depolarization would take much longer in the presence of TTX.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the TTX experiments.

claim: The pharmacological conditions under which the calcium propagation is best revealed are non-physiological.
source: The pharmacological conditions under which the calcium propagation is best revealed are non-physiological.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment by the authors about their experimental conditions.

claim: Under physiological conditions, the distance over which calcium needs to propagate is less due to participation of the action potential.
source: Instead, the distance over which calcium needs to propagate under physiological conditions is certainly less due to participation of the action potential.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of TTX and normal conditions.

claim: The P/Q channels participate in the calcium generation and the secondary sources for calcium are also near the boutons, minimizing the need for long distance propagation.
source: Additionally, as pointed out earlier the P/Q channels do participate in the calcium generation and the secondary sources for calcium are also near the boutons, minimizing the need for long distance propagation.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings and interpretation.

claim: All evidence points to a central involvement of the secondary source of calcium in the delayed onset of asynchronous release.
source: However, all evidence points to a central involvement of this secondary source of calcium in the delayed onset of asynchronous release.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion based on all their experimental findings.

claim: The finding of a robust propagating calcium signal in the motor neuron was unexpected.
source: Our finding of a robust propagating calcium signal in the motor neuron was quite unexpected.
evidence: This is the authors' statement about the novelty of their finding.

claim: Published accounts of propagating calcium signals have been largely limited to postsynaptic cells.
source: Published accounts of propagating calcium signals like those shown in our study have been largely limited to postsynaptic cells (Ross, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature supported by a citation.

claim: There is precedence for ryanodine-sensitive calcium stores involvement in synaptic transmission at guinea pig sympathetic nerve terminals and frog NMJ.
source: However, there is some precedence for ryanodine-sensitive calcium stores involvement in synaptic transmission at guinea pig sympathetic nerve terminals and frog NMJ (Smith and Cunnane, 1996; Narita et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The findings provide a clearer understanding of the delayed onset and persistent release properties associated with asynchronous release.
source: Consequently, we have a clearer understanding of the delayed onset and persistent release properties associated with asynchronous release.
evidence: This is the authors' conclusion about the significance of their findings.

claim: It will be critical to determine whether similar mechanisms are at work at synapses within the central nervous system.
source: In light of the ubiquitous nature of asynchronous release, it will be critical to determine whether similar mechanisms are at work at synapses within the central nervous system.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions based on the findings.

claim: Zebrafish were maintained between the ages of 72–96 hr post-fertilization (hpf) for all experiments.
source: The electrophysiology and imaging experiments were performed exclusively on larva between the ages of 72–96 hr post-fertilization (hpf).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Tol2 transposon system was used to generate the transgenic fish line expressing synaptopHluorin in the CaP motor neuron.
source: The Tol2 transposon system was used to generate the transgenic fish line expressing synaptopHluorin in the CaP motor neuron.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: SynaptopHluorin was constructed by fusing super-ecliptic pHluorin to C-terminus of the zebrafish Vamp2 with an 8-amino acid linker.
source: SynaptopHluorin was constructed by fusing super-ecliptic pHluorin (Miesenbock et al., 1998) in frame to C-terminus of the zebrafish Vamp2 with an 8-amino acid linker.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.
